explanation: A well-formed model uses proper notation, names every entity, provides identifiers, and records relationships clearly. The other choices emphasize implementation shortcuts, temporary labels, or process design rather than model quality.

options.text: Every entity is named, each has an identifier, and the relationships are shown clearly.
The diagram includes only the tables that will likely be cheapest to implement.
Each entity is given a temporary code name so the model can be finalized later.
The model focuses on screen flows because that helps users understand the design.

prompt: A team sketches an ER diagram for a subscription service. Which choice best makes the model well-formed?

explanation: A well-formed model must name every entity, use clear labels, and show relationships. Missing names, ambiguous labels, and omitted relationships are all well-formedness problems. The other options refer to different concerns such as detail level, fidelity, or physical design.

options.text: The model is not well-formed because it has naming and relationship defects.
The model is too detailed because it includes too many attributes.
The model is high-fidelity because it reflects real business language.
The model is normalized incorrectly because it needs more indexes.

prompt: A reviewer says a draft data model is hard to use because one entity is unnamed, another is labeled with a vague business phrase, and one relationship is missing. What quality problem is the reviewer pointing to?

explanation: High-fidelity models accurately reflect relevant real-world relationships and constraints. If split deliveries can occur but the model leaves that out, the model is not faithful to the business context. The other choices describe physical design or other database topics, not model fidelity.

options.text: High fidelity, because the model does not reflect an important real-world relationship.
Well-formedness, because every model must always have physical table names.
Normalization, because split deliveries require more foreign keys.
Index design, because route splits affect query speed first.

prompt: A logistics company models deliveries but forgets to represent that some deliveries can be split across multiple routes. Which quality goal is most clearly being missed?

explanation: A is correct because a high-fidelity model should match the real business context, including the fact that one customer can hold several plans and one plan can apply to many customers. Modeling that many-to-many relationship preserves the stated facts. B loses valid multiple-plan cases, C collapses two different real-world things into one entity, and D fails to represent an important business relationship at all.

options.text: Model a many-to-many relationship between Customer and Plan.
Store a single Plan attribute in Customer because one current plan is enough for modeling.
Merge Customer and Plan into one entity because they both belong to the membership system.
Omit the relationship until physical database design decides how to store it.

prompt: A membership business has customers and plans. The business rules say a customer may hold multiple plans at the same time, and each plan may be held by many customers. In a conceptual data model, which choice best preserves a high-fidelity representation of this situation?

explanation: Well-formedness is about the model being properly named, identified, and structured. High fidelity is about accurately reflecting the real context, including constraints and exceptions. If the diagram is clear but misses a rule about mandatory assignment to one carrier, it can still be well-formed while falling short on fidelity.

options.text: It is well-formed but not fully high-fidelity because a relevant business constraint is missing.
It is high-fidelity but not well-formed because constraints are part of naming.
It is neither well-formed nor high-fidelity because every missing rule makes the diagram invalid.
It is complete because identifiers matter more than constraints.

prompt: A team presents a data model that uses clear entity names and identifiers, but it omits a rule that a shipment must belong to exactly one carrier. How should the model be judged?
